## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Conclusion (possible)
The evidence supports only a bounded answer: Elijah Wilkins died after 1870 and before the 1885 term of the Muhlenberg County court, most likely in or near Muhlenberg County, Kentucky. An exact date and place of death are not established by the evidence gathered so far; they remain unresolved pending the 1880 census, the original estate papers and burial records.

## Evidence
**Lower bound.** Elijah Wilkins was alive in 1870 per existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, 1870), the end of his census trail. F2 carries no linked source entry in research.json.

**Upper bound.** The Muhlenberg County Court order books record the administration of the intestate estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, with Jesse Wilkins as administrator, 1885 term (Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org). This is a derivative source (a full-text index of the order-book page; the original was not separately imaged), and its information is indeterminate: the clerk is the informant, with unknown proximity to the death. The death itself is inferred, not stated, so the entry bounds the death and gives no date. Place: the record establishes where the estate was administered, not where he died.

**Identity.** The decedent is tied to our subject by the administrator, Jesse Wilkins, who is the subject's son in the tree (R1). This is an inference from a shared name, place and kinship, not an explicit statement of relationship in the record, so identity is probable and not certain. No competing Elijah Wilkins candidate has been recorded, and no conflicts are open.

**Documented negative.** No Kentucky death certificate exists for him: statewide registration began in 1911, decades after he died, and the search of the statewide death collections returned nothing (12 results examined).

## Why possible
The source is derivative with indeterminate information and an inferred link. The 1870-1885 bracket is 15 years wide, and a reachable record not yet searched, the 1880 census, could narrow it directly. Untested alternatives for a place and date are the original order book and estate papers, and cemetery records. The bracket is encoded in the tree because the death is not in doubt, only its date.

Proofs are never final; new evidence may change this answer.

## Question
What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

## Conclusion
**Not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not establish Ellen's maiden surname. It is not established by the evidence gathered so far and remains unresolved pending the records named below.

## Evidence
The only record gathered is the Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate of Michael Doyle and Ellen, 12 June 1889, cited as: "Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch." (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDOYLE-1889). It is an original source. The marriage itself is documented by primary, directly stated information from the couple themselves reporting to the recorder: the groom's name is Michael Doyle and the bride's given name is Ellen. The bride's surname, and her parents' names, are illegible in the register image because of the clerk's hand and fading. The question's own surname target therefore has no usable direct evidence, and no indirect evidence has been gathered. Both spouses are linked to the tree persons Ellen Doyle (I1) and Michael Doyle (I2). No conflicts exist.

## Why the tier is not higher
There is no candidate surname to weigh, so no preponderance exists in any direction. The search has so far covered one repository and one record. Records that could independently name Ellen's maiden surname, listed in the search summary, are unsearched: a second transcription of the register or the Iowa marriage index, the 1900 and 1910 censuses and 1895 and 1905 Iowa state censuses, the birth and death records of the couple's children, Ellen's death record and obituary, Dubuque parish registers, and 1889 Dubuque newspapers. Although the question carries an exhaustiveness declaration, its own stop criteria show a single repository and no independent verification, so the declaration does not describe a finished search. This conclusion is open to revision as these records are searched.

## Tree
No fact or relationship was added: nothing here establishes a surname value to encode. The marriage itself is already represented by Couple I1-I2.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) most probably married Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX) on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway.

## Evidence

The FamilySearch index "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926" holds an entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway, citing the Hamre prestegjeld parish register. Citation: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register.

The index is a derivative of the church book. The information it carries (names, date, place) is primary and direct: the officiating minister or parish clerk recorded the marriage as part of official duty, and the parties themselves are the named subjects. The groom's name matches the tree person exactly, and the marriage took place in Hamre, the parish where he was christened on 7 April 1759 (tree fact anders-christening-1). The bride is indexed as "Urna Halsteinsdr", a transcription variant of "Unna Halsteinsdatter". The surname form matches, and her christening on 27 May 1745 at Hamre (tree fact unna-christening-1) fits the same parish. The tree already joined the couple (relationship rel-anders-unna) but carried no marriage date or place.

## Conflicts and limits

No conflicting evidence exists and no conflict is registered. The bride was about 41 and the groom about 27. This is unusual but not implausible, and no other record disputes it. The bride's name rests on an index transcription, not on an examined image. The conclusion rests on one derivative index entry. The church book original was not examined, and the index shows no image. These gaps keep the conclusion below proved. Civil registration did not exist in 1786, so the church book is the only contemporaneous record type for the marriage.

## What could raise it

The digitized Hamre church book page for 1786 would show the original entry and confirm the bride's name form. Parish banns or any later record naming the couple as spouses would corroborate it.

**Tier: probable.**

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? An unsourced online family tree names him as the father.

## Conclusion (disproved)
Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was not Patrick Flynn's father. He was buried on 14 November 1842, more than a year before the earliest plausible birth date of Patrick and roughly three years before the best estimate (~1845).

## Evidence
**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842 (original record; primary information, entered by the officiating priest in the course of duty; direct evidence of death). The entry's identifiers (townland, age about 42, wife Bridget) match the Thomas Flynn the online tree describes, so this is the man the claim refers to. Source: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Patrick's birth.** The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present (original record; informant unidentified, so the quality of the age is indeterminate; indirect evidence of birth, about 1845). Source: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The 1908 death certificate, informant his son-in-law James Brown (secondary information, not present at the birth), gives age about 63 on 12 March 1908, so birth about 1845. Source: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026. The certificate (a different informant, nearly sixty years later) agrees with the census. Neither record names a father.

## Correlation
Both age statements are inferred, so each could be off by a year or two. Even so, the census (age 5 in 1850) and the certificate (age 63 in March 1908) fit a birth no earlier than about 1844, more than a year after Thomas's burial. Allowing generous age error does not close that gap. The sources do not conflict, and no conflict is registered.

## Limits
The conclusion rests on the burial being that of the man the tree names. That identification uses townland, age and wife's name, which are consistent with the tree's description. The finding refutes this candidate only. It does not identify Patrick's father. The 1850 household headed by the widow Bridget Flynn is a lead, but nothing gathered ties her to Thomas of Ballingarry. Records that could identify Patrick's actual parents include a baptismal record, a marriage record, Bridget Flynn's own records, and later census households.

The unsourced online tree claim is refuted by primary evidence and should not be carried into our tree. Proofs are never final, but no evidence now known could make a man buried in 1842 the father of a child born in 1844 or later.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) married Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX) on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway. The evidence strongly indicates this; it is rated probable rather than proved because it rests on one derivative index entry and the register page itself has not been examined.

## Evidence

The FamilySearch index entry "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway, cites the Hamre prestegjeld parish register. It names the groom as Anders Monsen and the bride as "Urna Halsteinsdr", and gives the date and place as above. Source citation: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register.

Classification: the index is a derivative of the church book. The underlying register entry was made by the officiating minister or parish clerk in the course of official duty, so its information on the date, place and parties is primary, and the evidence is direct.

## Identity

The groom matches Anders Monsen exactly by name and sex, and Hamre is the parish where he was christened on 7 April 1759 (tree fact anders-christening-1). The bride's indexed name "Urna Halsteinsdr" is a transcription variant of Unna Halsteinsdatter (the abbreviated patronymic and u/n confusion are common in indexing). Her christening at Hamre on 27 May 1745 (tree fact unna-christening-1) fits, and the tree already carried a Couple relationship between them. At the marriage he was about 27 and she about 41, which is plausible. No conflicting record exists.

## Digitized image

The request was to state that the register image is digitized and accessible on FamilySearch. The project data do not support that. The search response carried no image reference, no image count was reported, and the entry was never opened with a record read. The URL above is the record-level index ARK, not a confirmed image ARK. This conclusion therefore describes the source as an index-only entry. Whether an image of the Hamre register page exists should be checked directly.

## Limits

The tree facts on the persons (birth, christening, death, burial) carry no linked source entries in research.json; they were used only for the identity check. The only unchecked item is the original register page, which would raise the evidence from derivative to original. No other record type is known for an 1786 Norwegian marriage. Evidence may be reassessed if new records appear.

- Lancashire baptism indexes (Ancestry, Lancashire Online Parish Clerks)
- Lancashire nonconformist registers
- LDS membership records (~1837–1839)
- 1841 census for Ashton-under-Lyne
- Preston baptisms for 1832–1833

FamilySearch collection 1465701 (England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910) indexes Lancashire parish registers including Ashton-under-Lyne's St. Michael and All Angels. An Anglican christening register entry for this period names the father's full name, father's occupation, and mother's Christian name — the most direct path to naming John's parents. This collection is free and the highest-probability first search.

Cross-check of the same christening event using Ancestry collection 2575 (Lancashire, England, Church of England Births & Baptisms, 1813-1911, index & images). Ancestry's indexing is independent of FamilySearch's and may surface the record if the FamilySearch index has a name transcription error or if the record is in the images but not the FamilySearch index.

Lancashire Online Parish Clerks (lan-opc.org.uk) provides free transcription abstracts from many Ashton-area registers — 9.5 million Lancashire records as of 2018. This free index may yield the christening entry and its parent names without a paid subscription, and its transcriptions derive from original registers independently of FamilySearch/Ancestry.

Once the christening names a father, the parents' marriage record is required to establish the mother's maiden name and corroborate the parentage identification. Lancashire parish registers (FS collection 1465701) cover marriages from 1538-1910. The parents married by approximately 1832 at the latest; searching for a Richardson marriage in Lancashire in the years before 1833 would name both parents. Per planning standards, a dedicated parents-marriage item is required for parentage questions.

If the Anglican christening yields nothing, search FamilySearch collection 3656808 (England, Lancashire Non-Conformist Church Records, 1647-1996, index & images, free). Ashton-under-Lyne had a significant Nonconformist community; if the Richardson family were Methodists or other Dissenters (consistent with their receptiveness to LDS missionaries in 1837-1839), the christening would appear in a nonconformist register instead of the Anglican register.

The Richardson family converted to the LDS church in Lancashire approximately 1837-1839 (the family is documented in Nauvoo by 1839; LDS missionaries arrived in Lancashire in July 1837). LDS membership records and mission journals from this period, held at the Church History Library (Salt Lake City, Utah), may record the entire family unit — including parents' names, ages, and place of residence — at the time of conversion. This is an LDS-specific FAN avenue with high potential given the family's documented LDS affiliation.

John Richardson was in Nauvoo by 1839 and will not appear in the 1841 England census. However, his parents may still be in England in 1841 and appear as a Richardson household in Ashton-under-Lyne. If the christening has already named the father, this search can confirm identity and potentially name other children. FamilySearch indexes the 1841 England census free of charge.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Parentage of John Richardson (q_001): Argument

**Question.** What does the Ashton-under-Lyne parish christening register record for John Richardson, baptised 25 September (1833 per the tree), about his parentage?

**Conclusion (probable).** The original baptism register names the child's parents as Thomas Richardson, a spinner, and Mary. The evidence strongly suggests that John Richardson (tree person LR9N-VGQ, later of Nauvoo and Richmond, Utah) was the son of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu. The identification is probable rather than proved, for the reasons below. It was not stated as settled because one identifying attribute, the year, does not agree between the register and the tree.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908)?

**Conclusion (probable).** The evidence indicates that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. His mother is not identified by any record examined so far.

### Evidence for the father
1. **1908 death certificate** (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026). An original record that states 'Father: Thomas Flynn'. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at the birth, so the parentage is secondary information. It is the only direct statement of the relationship.
2. **1850 census** (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026). An original record. It lists Patrick in the household of Thomas Flynn. This census does not state relationships, so the link is inferred from household position and shared surname (indirect, informant unknown). An Ancestry index of the same census is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.
3. **1860 census** (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). An original record. It lists Patrick, aged 15, in Thomas Flynn's household. Again the relationship is inferred (indirect, informant unknown).

The three records come from different creators and dates and point the same way, but the two direct pieces of reasoning are weak individually: the censuses do not name the relationship, and the certificate rests on a secondary informant. Their agreement, with no contradicting record, is what supports a probable finding.

### Conflict accounted for
Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses versus Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favour of Ireland. The son-in-law was a distant, late informant for a birth fact. The dispute concerns Patrick's birthplace, not who his father was, and the household and surname match across all three records, so it does not undermine the identity link. Tree fact F1 (Birth, about 1845, Ireland) is consistent with this resolution.

### Why not higher
No record states the relationship from a first-hand informant. Thomas Flynn's probate, church baptism records, and the 1880 census (which gives relationships) have not been searched, and research has not been declared exhaustive. Hence probable, not proved.

### Mother
No examined record names a mother. Maternity is not established by the evidence gathered so far; it remains open pending a baptism record, Patrick's marriage record, or the 1870 and 1880 census households.

The finding is open to revision if new evidence emerges.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

The online-tree claim that Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, was the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) does not hold up. Thomas was buried nearly three years before Patrick was born. This conclusion is **disproved** for this candidate only. It says nothing yet about who Patrick's parents actually were.

## The claim

Several online family trees, citing no record, name Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry (born about 1800, wife Bridget) as Patrick's father. The test is whether primary records are compatible with that.

## Evidence

**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn, of Ballingarry, on 14 November 1842. The entry was made by the officiating priest as a contemporaneous register entry, so it is original and primary information. The townland, approximate age (about 42) and wife Bridget in the entry match the man the trees name, which establishes that this is the intended Thomas. Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Patrick's birth.** Two independent original sources give his age. (1) The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present, implying birth about 1845. The informant is unknown, so the age is of indeterminate quality and indirect. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. (2) His death certificate gives death on 12 March 1908 at about age 63, implying birth about 1845. The death date is primary information from the attending physician. The age was supplied by his son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth, so it is secondary. Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026.

## Correlation

The two age statements agree with each other and are independent informants (an unknown household member in 1850, the son-in-law in 1908). Neither names a parent; both are indirect evidence for the birth year. A father who was buried in November 1842 could have fathered Patrick only if Patrick had been born posthumously, no later than about August 1843. Both ages would then have to be wrong by about two years in the same direction. Ages in these records do drift by a year or so, but not consistently by two or more years across two unrelated informants, so a pre-burial conception is not a credible reading. No conflict exists among the sources, and none is registered.

The same evidence also fits Bridget Flynn as Patrick's widowed mother in 1850. It does not show that she is the Bridget married to Thomas of Ballingarry, and that link has not been tested.

## Limits

The finding rests on indirect birth evidence set against a direct death record. It refutes only the Ballingarry Thomas. A baptism entry for Patrick, a Pennsylvania naturalization or church record, or an obituary could name his real parents. Such records could change who the parents were, but not the result for this candidate.

**Assessment of ps\_001 against the GPS — q\_001 (Parentage of Patrick Flynn)**

---

## Verdict: `probable` tier is justified; GPS *proved* is not yet reached

The existing tier of **probable** is correct and defensible. The proof does not rise to *proved* for three reasons: census evidence is indirect, the death certificate informant is secondary, and the search is not yet reasonably exhaustive. The tier is not merely *possible* — three sources consistently point to Thomas Flynn as father and nothing contradicts it.

**A significant framing gap:** the question asks for *both* parents. The proof addresses only the father. The mother is never mentioned, not even with "mother not identified." A per-claim breakdown (paternity probable; maternity not proved) would be more accurate.

---

## Component-by-Component Review

### GPS 1 — Reasonably Exhaustive Research: **not met (correctly acknowledged as a gap)**

- The 1850 and 1860 censuses were searched; the **1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses were not**. The 1880 census is the first U.S. federal census to record stated relationships and would directly address paternity — and potentially identify the mother.
- The proof summary says "probate search in progress," but the narrative says probate was not located and there is no probate search log entry. Those two statements conflict.

### GPS 2 — Complete and Accurate Citations: **met**

- Each cited record is named with date, place, and an inline citation matching the stored source entries.
- Informant analysis is present for each source.

### GPS 3 — Analysis and Correlation: **mostly met**

- All three cited assertions (a\_004, a\_010, a\_013) carry classification, informant, basis, and quality.
- Three wording issues:
  1. "Three independent lines of evidence" overstates independence — both censuses likely rest on the same household informant.
  2. The narrative says census informants were "likely present in the household"; stored classification says informant unknown, quality indeterminate.
  3. The narrative does not confirm whether Thomas Flynn (~32 in 1850) is the same man in the 1860 household.

### GPS 4 — Resolution of Conflicting Evidence: **met**

- Conflict c\_001 (birthplace: Ireland in censuses vs. Pennsylvania on death certificate) is resolved and cited. Preferring two contemporaneous census entries over a secondary informant is sound genealogical reasoning.
- One weakness: the two census entries likely share one informant, which should temper the confidence to "Ireland accepted as likely" rather than certain.

### GPS 5 — Soundly Reasoned, Coherently Written Conclusion: **partially met**

- The narrative is coherent and self-contained.
- The conclusion is weakened by the independence overstatement and by the absence of any claim about the mother.

---

## Evidence Gaps for the Next Round (not defects in ps\_001 as it stands)

These sources exist in research.json but are not yet cited in ps\_001. They are unread/unextracted — gaps for future work:

| Source | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **src\_005** — St. Mary's baptism register, Pottsville, 1845 | Highest priority. Primary record of parentage; may name both parents; bears on Ireland vs. Pennsylvania birthplace. If it names Thomas, the father claim could reach *proved* once exhaustiveness is established. |
| **src\_006** — Will of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County, 1881 | Direct evidence if Patrick is named as son; may also name a wife (the mother). |
| **src\_008** — Deed, Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn, 1881 | Shows a relationship; relationship wording may or may not be stated. |
| **src\_009** — Patrick Flynn obituary, Pottsville Republican, 1908 | May list survivors or name parents. |
| **1870, 1880, 1900 censuses** | Not yet searched. 1880 is highest priority (stated relationships). |

**Would they change the tier?** Yes — src\_005 (baptism) and src\_006 (will) have potential to lift the father claim to *proved* and to open the mother question. That work belongs to the next research cycle, not to a revision of this proof.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. Extract and classify **src\_005, src\_006, src\_008, src\_009**.
2. Search the **1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses** (route through research-plan).
3. After extraction and census work, **re-conclude ps\_001** with separate claims for father (currently probable) and mother (currently not proved).

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Assessment of ps_001 (q_001, parentage of Patrick Flynn). No new proof was written.**

**Verdict:** The tier of `probable` is justified. The proof does not meet the Genealogical Proof Standard (GPS) at `proved`. It names Thomas Flynn as father only, and the question asks for both parents.

**1. Tier.**
- `probable` is right, and `proved` is blocked by three things. The census evidence is indirect, the death certificate informant is secondary, and the search is not reasonably exhaustive.
- The tier is not `possible`. Three sources, each placing Patrick with or naming Thomas, point the same way, and no source contradicts the father.
- The proof answers only the father. The mother is not addressed, and the narrative never says "mother not identified". The question asks "who were the parents", so a per-claim breakdown (paternity probable, maternity not proved) would be more accurate.

**2. Self-containment and citations.**
- The narrative is self-contained. It names each record, its date and place, and gives inline citations that match the stored source entries word for word.
- It gives the informant analysis for each source. It describes the death certificate as "direct evidence" but classifies the informant as secondary, which is correct.
- Three wording points should be fixed.
  - "Three independent lines of evidence" overstates independence. The two censuses rest on household position and likely the same informant, and the conflict record itself notes this.
  - The narrative says the census informants were "likely present in the household". The stored classification says informant unknown, quality indeterminate.
  - The narrative does not say whether Thomas Flynn is the same man in both census households (age ~32 in 1850, born ~1818). The supporting person link for the 1860 household is not stated.

**3. Component 3, analysis and correlation (mostly met).**
- All three cited assertions (a_004, a_010, a_013) are classified for quality, informant and basis. The links for Patrick and Thomas are in place.
- The census links rest on inference from household position. The 1850 and 1860 relationships are "child_inferred", with basis "inferred" and quality indeterminate. The narrative says so.
- The death certificate is the only source that states the relationship.

**4. Conflicts.**
- The single conflict (c_001, birthplace Ireland in the censuses versus Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved and cited.
- Birthplace is an identifying attribute, so the resolution matters. Preferring two contemporary census entries over one informant who was not a witness is reasoned, and it is sound.
- It is weakened because the two census entries probably share one informant. The narrative should say Ireland is accepted as likely rather than certain.
- The tree matches this. Patrick's primary Birth fact (F1) is Ireland, about 1845.
- The question and objective still say "born in Pennsylvania". This is a mismatch in the framing, not a defect in the proof.

**5. Exhaustiveness (not met, correctly acknowledged).**
- The proof lists what was searched: the 1850 census on FamilySearch, Ancestry and MyHeritage, the 1860 census, and the 1908 death certificate.
- Two points need correcting.
  - The search summary says "probate search in progress", while the narrative says probate was not located. The log has no probate entry.

# Assessment of ps_001 (q_001 — Parentage of Patrick Flynn)

**Overall verdict:** ps_001 does not yet meet the Genealogical Proof Standard, but its **"Probable" tier is appropriate and justified**. The shortfall is honest. Several mechanical defects need fixing before a revised proof can fully comply.

---

## GPS Component-by-Component Assessment

### 1. Reasonably Exhaustive Research — ❌ Not Met
- Cited evidence covers only the 1850 and 1860 censuses (src_001, src_003) and the 1908 death certificate (src_004).
- The proof's own search summary acknowledges the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and a probate search is "in progress."
- No `search_stop` has been declared on q_001 — exhaustiveness has not been asserted.
- Four additional sources in the project (will, deed, obituary, baptism) are uncited and unextracted.

### 2. Complete and Accurate Source Citations — ⚠️ Partly Met
- The underlying stored citations for src_001, src_003, and src_004 are sound.
- The narrative cites evidence only by bare IDs (e.g., "a_004, a_010, a_013," "src_001"). A reader without the project files cannot identify the records, their dates, or their repositories. This fails the self-containment test.

### 3. Analysis and Correlation — ❌ Weak
- The narrative never classifies the evidence. The two censuses are **original sources with indirect evidence** (they don't state relationships; parentage is inferred from household position and shared surname). The death certificate is an **original source with direct but secondary information** (the informant, Patrick's son-in-law James Brown, was not present at the birth).
- Nothing cited is both primary and direct.
- The narrative merely says the assertions are "consistent with" parentage, without showing the reasoning.
- The Ancestry 1850 index (src_002) is derivative and not independent of the FamilySearch image — the narrative does not note this.

### 4. Conflict Resolution — ⚠️ Addressed by Pointer Only
- c_001 (birthplace conflict: Ireland in censuses vs. Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in the conflict entry, with reasonable reasoning.
- The narrative says only "see the conflict entry" — that fails self-containment. The resolution must be incorporated into the narrative itself.
- The tree records Ireland as Patrick's primary birthplace, while the question says Pennsylvania. The narrative does not address this discrepancy.

### 5. Soundly Reasoned, Coherent Conclusion — ❌ Not Met
- The narrative provides no genuine argument — no reasoning chain, no tier rationale beyond "not all direct" and "plan items outstanding."
- **Crucially, only the father is addressed.** The question asks for *parents*, and no mother is identified or even discussed. This gap should be stated explicitly.
- "Probably the son of Thomas Flynn" is supported by the evidence cited — the tier is correct, the conclusion language is appropriate.

---

## Tier

**Probable is correct.** The indirect census evidence is consistent across two censuses (1850 and 1860), and one stated, secondary source names Thomas. Nothing contradicts the relationship, and the open conflict is resolved. **Proved is blocked** by: indirect and secondary evidence only; no mother identified; no exhaustiveness declaration; and thin narrative reasoning. Lowering to "Possible" is unwarranted — the unsearched records would mostly corroborate what is already in hand.

---

## Evidence Gaps for the Next Round *(not defects of ps_001 as written)*

These exist in the project but are **not cited in ps_001** and have no extracted assertions:

| Source | Why It Matters | Tier Impact |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| **1845 baptism, St. Mary's, Pottsville (src_005)** | Closest to direct, primary evidence; would likely name both parents | Could raise tier; also bears on the birthplace conflict |
| **1881 will of Thomas Flynn (src_006)** | Direct, primary evidence of heirs; may identify the mother | Strongest item; could lift toward Proved |
| **1881 deed, Thomas to Patrick (src_008)** | Indirect corroboration of the relationship | Corroborating, but not tier-changing alone |
| **1908 obituary, Pottsville Republican (src_009)** | May name parents or surviving siblings; independent informant | Corroborating |
| **1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses** | 1880 census states relationships directly — would give stated rather than inferred evidence | Meaningful corroboration |

Note: the baptism, will, deed, and obituary all carry rough working citations that need completing (missing volume/page locators, creator names, dates) before they can be cited in a revised proof.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Extract and classify the 1845 baptism and 1881 will first** — these have the highest potential to change the tier.
2. **Re-run proof-conclusion on q_001** to update ps_001 in place, with a rewritten, self-contained narrative that includes: named records with inline citations, explicit information-quality classifications, the c_001 reasoning within the text, and a statement about the mother.
3. **Plan the 1880 census search** via research-plan.
4. **Fix the rough citations** on src_005, src_006, src_008, and src_009.

---

**Summary finding:** Patrick Flynn was probably the son of Thomas Flynn. The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Patrick in Thomas's household, and the 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father — but neither census states the relationship, and the death-certificate informant was secondary. The mother is unidentified. Research is not yet exhaustive. The tier is correct; the narrative needs to be rewritten to be self-contained and to meet GPS components 2–5.

   - The narrative names evidence only by bare ids ("a_004, a_010, a_013", "src_001, src_003, src_004", "c_001", "plan_001"). This is a failure of self-containment, not a style issue. A reader without the project files cannot tell what the records are, their dates, or where they are held.

3. **Analysis and correlation: weak in the write-up.**
   - The narrative never classifies the evidence. The classifications exist in the assertions, but the narrative omits them.
   - a_004 (1850 census) and a_010 (1860 census) are inferred, indirect evidence. Neither census states relationships. Both rest on household position and shared surname, and both have indeterminate information quality.
   - a_013 (death certificate, "Father: Thomas Flynn") is the only stated parentage. It is secondary information from a son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at the birth.
   - The two censuses are original sources with indirect evidence. The death certificate is original with direct but secondary information. Nothing here is primary and direct.
   - The narrative says only that the assertions are "consistent with" parentage. It does not show the reasoning, for example that Patrick appears as a child in the same household at both censuses.
   - The narrative does not mention that Ancestry's 1850 index (src_002) is derivative and not independent of src_001.

4. **Conflict resolution: addressed, but only by pointer.**
   - c_001 is the birthplace conflict: Ireland in the censuses against Pennsylvania on the 1908 death certificate. The conflict entry is resolved, and its reasoning is reasonable.
   - The narrative gives no reasoning of its own: it says only "see the conflict entry". That fails the self-containment test.
   - Birthplace bears on whether the census Patrick and the death-certificate Patrick are the same man. The resolution rests on the death-certificate informant being secondary.
   - The narrative should say this openly and should name the shared-informant weakness that the conflict entry itself concedes.
   - The tree currently records Ireland as Patrick's primary birthplace, while the question and objective say Pennsylvania. The narrative does not note this either.

5. **Soundly reasoned, coherent conclusion: not met.**
   - The narrative gives no real argument. It also gives no tier rationale beyond "not all direct" and "plan items outstanding".
   - "Probably" is appropriate phrasing for the tier. The conclusion itself ("Probably the son of Thomas Flynn") is supported.
   - Only the father is addressed. The question asks for parents, and no mother is identified or discussed.
   - The narrative should state this limit explicitly and name a record that could still identify the mother.

## Tier

Probable is right. The indirect census evidence is consistent across 1850 and 1860, and one stated, secondary source names Thomas. Nothing contradicts the relationship, and the open conflict is resolved. Proved is blocked by four things:
- indirect and secondary evidence only;
- no mother identified;
- no exhaustiveness declaration;
- the narrative's thin reasoning.

I would not lower it to "possible", because the unsearched records would mostly corroborate an answer that is already in hand.

## Other checks

- **Tree:** the ParentChild link from Thomas Flynn (I2) to Patrick Flynn (I1) is encoded as R1, which is correct for probable. R1 cites S1, S2 and S3, but S2 is the 1860 census source entry, which is fine. One oddity: src_001 and src_002 both map to S1, so the Ancestry index and the FamilySearch image share one tree source entry.
- **Question status:** the question is still stored as `in_progress`, while ps_001 reads as concluded. The status line says "concluded while blocked: re-conclude ps_001". Re-concluding is the right next step, and the question should stay open until it is.
- **Identity links:** Patrick (I1) and Thomas (I2) each carry at least one linked identity assertion (pe_001, pe_003), so the preconditions gate is satisfied.
- **Unclear scope of "plan_001":** the narrative leans on it, but the proof never lists what its outstanding items are.

## Evidence gaps for the next round (not defects of ps_001)

These are in the project but not cited in ps_001. All have empty assertion counts, so they have not been extracted.

- **1881 will of Thomas Flynn (src_006).** This is probably the strongest item. A will naming Patrick, and possibly a wife, as heirs could give direct, primary evidence of parentage and could identify the mother. It could lift the tier toward proved and could narrow the answer, since it addresses the missing mother.
- **1881 deed, Thomas to Patrick (src_008).** It shows a transfer between the two men, which is indirect support. It would corroborate parentage, but a deed alone would not raise the tier far.
- **1908 obituary, Pottsville Republican (src_009).** It may name the parents or surviving siblings. It is probably a secondary source, but it would add an independent informant.
- **1845 baptism, St. Mary's, Pottsville (src_005).** If it matches, a baptismal register would be the closest to direct, primary evidence of parentage and would likely name both parents. It could raise the tier. Its Pottsville, Pennsylvania location would also bear on the birthplace conflict, since the censuses say Ireland.
- **1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn (src_007).** This one is peripheral to Patrick's parentage. It may be a descendant's record, which would help identity but not parentage.
- **1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses.** The 1880 census is the first to state relationships directly, so it would give stated rather than inferred evidence of the household relationship. It could help as corroboration.
- **Probate and estate records.** These are in progress and would support the will.

Four of the sources above (the baptism, will, deed and obituary) also carry rough working citations that need completing. They are missing volume and page locators, correct creator names, and dates. Those need fixing before they can be cited in a revised proof.

## Recommended next step

Extract and classify the 1845 baptism and 1881 will first, then re-run proof-conclusion on q_001 to update ps_001 in place. The narrative should be rewritten so that it is self-contained: named records, inline citations copied from the source entries, explicit information-quality classifications, its own c_001 reasoning, and a statement about the mother. Planning for the baptism, will and 1880 census belongs in research-plan.

---

The finding is that Patrick Flynn was probably the son of Thomas Flynn. Patrick is listed in Thomas's household in the 1850 and 1860 censuses, and his 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father. The censuses do not state relationships, so they only suggest the link. The death certificate was filled in by Patrick's son-in-law, who was not a firsthand witness. The mother is not identified. It is likely, but not firmly established. Not yet searched are the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses, probate records and the cited-but-unread church baptism, will, deed and obituary.

Next, the baptism, will, deed and obituary should be read and added to the evidence, and the written conclusion should be rewritten to be self-contained.

## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Status: not concluded; identity link to the tree person is not yet established

The only dated evidence is a derivative index of the Muhlenberg County Court order book, 1885 term, naming Jesse Wilkins administrator of the intestate estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased ("Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org."). It shows an Elijah Wilkins was dead by 1885; it gives no death date. Its informant is an unidentified court clerk, so information quality is indeterminate and the death bound is indirect.

Existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, 1870) shows the subject was alive in 1870, giving a lower bound; F2 carries no linked source entry in the project. The tree also links Jesse Wilkins (I2) as the subject's son (R1), but no assertion is linked to Jesse as a person, and the administrator assertion is linked only to Elijah. A second Elijah Wilkins, born about 1822 in Muhlenberg County, is a recorded namesake and could be the decedent. Whether the administrator Jesse is the subject's son, and so whether the estate is the subject's, is therefore untested.

Because Jesse Wilkins is the sole link between the estate and the subject and has no linked identity evidence, the identity precondition is not met and no conclusion is drawn. Nothing is written to the tree. Not established by the evidence so far: the estate's ownership and the death date. Linking Jesse's identity (his parentage, from a census household or other record naming him with Elijah) and examining the order-book image or estate file could settle both.

Would-be bounded finding, held for after identity is settled: died after 1870 and before 1885 in Muhlenberg County; no Kentucky death certificate exists (statewide registration began 1911).

## Proof Conclusion — Patrick Flynn's Parentage (q_001)

**Proof summary `ps_001` has been written and saved as a Proof Argument.**

---

### Tier: **Probable** (shortfall: *gap*)

Paternity is **probable**; maternity is **not proved**. Question `q_001` remains open because Patrick's mother is unidentified and research has not yet been declared exhaustive.

---

### Findings

**Paternity (Thomas Flynn → Patrick Flynn):**
- The **1908 death certificate** names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, but the informant was a son-in-law, making this *secondary information*.
- The **1850 and 1860 censuses** show Patrick living in Thomas's household, but neither record states family relationships — parentage is *inferred*, not stated.
- Birthplace conflict `c_001` is resolved and does not block the conclusion.
- A ParentChild relationship (R1) linking Thomas Flynn (I2) → Patrick Flynn (I1) has been added to the tree, citing the death certificate (S3, quality 2) and both censuses (S1 & S2, quality 1).

**Maternity (unresolved):**
- Bridget Flynn (I3) is linked to the family only by an 1870 widow entry and a shared surname (match score: 0.0002).
- Pottsville baptism records name Patrick's *wife* as Mary Doyle — not his mother.
- Hypothesis h_002's naming-pattern argument was not counted as evidence.

---

### Records Still Unsearched
- Thomas Flynn's **probate/estate file**
- Patrick's **marriage record**
- A **birth or baptism record** (~1845)
- Thomas's **burial record**

Any of these could name Patrick's mother.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Run **research-exhaustiveness** on `q_001` to formally assess whether searches to date are adequate.
2. Use **research-plan** to target the four record types above, which are most likely to identify the mother.

# Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. c. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Question.** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn? **Answer.** The evidence supports Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father (probable). It does not identify his mother (not proved).

## Paternity: Thomas Flynn (probable)

Three sources point to Thomas Flynn, and they are not equal in weight.

1. **1908 death certificate (direct evidence, secondary information).** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. It is an original record. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth and was reporting what he had been told about his father-in-law's parentage. It names Thomas Flynn as father. This is the only record that states the relationship outright, and its information is secondary.
2. **1850 census (indirect evidence, indeterminate information).** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. A Patrick Flynn is enumerated in the household of Thomas Flynn (head). The 1850 census does not record relationships, so the parent-child reading is inferred from household position and shared surname. (An Ancestry index of the same census is a derivative copy and adds no independent weight.)
3. **1860 census (indirect evidence, indeterminate information).** 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household. Relationships were not recorded in 1860 either. The two censuses are separate enumerations, but the same household reporting probably lies behind both, and both rest on the same inference.

The three sources agree and nothing contradicts them. The censuses place Patrick, a child in 1850, under Thomas's roof ten years running, and the later death certificate independently names the same man as father. Because the censuses are indirect and the one direct statement is secondary, the case is strong but short of proved.

**Conflict accounted for.** Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the 1850 and 1860 censuses against Pennsylvania on the 1908 death certificate) is resolved in favour of Ireland, the death certificate informant being a son-in-law reporting 63 years after the birth. The dispute concerns where Patrick was born, not whether the census Patrick and the decedent are one man; the death certificate's Pennsylvania birthplace is the one detail on which the son-in-law's reliability is weakest, and this lowers, slightly, the weight on his statement of Thomas as father. It is one reason the tier is not higher. Nothing in the conflict points to a different father.

## Maternity: not proved

Content note: none of the evidence is sensitive, but the mother question is open and no candidate is established.

The candidate is Bridget Flynn (I3), who appears in the 1870 census as a widow, age 52, head of household (1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026). Her link rests only on the shared surname and widowhood. 'Flynn' is a common surname in the county, no record names her husband, no record names her as Thomas's wife or Patrick's mother, and no child is in her household. The identity link has a match score of 0.0002 and is rated speculative. Thomas Flynn does not appear in the 1870 census, which fits a death before 1870, but that is equally true of any widow of the surname. This is not evidence of a relationship.

The 1870 and 1872 baptisms at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville (Baptismal register 1868-1880; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026) name Patrick Flynn and Mary Doyle as parents of Patrick's own children. They identify Patrick's wife, not his mother, and name no grandparent, so they give no support to Bridget as mother. The mother therefore remains unidentified. Patrick's marriage record, Thomas Flynn's estate or burial record, or a record of Patrick's birth around 1845 could name her; these are unsearched.

## Tier and limits

Paternity is **probable**: three agreeing sources, one direct but secondary, two indirect, no contradiction. It is not proved because the evidence is indirect or secondary, the exhaustiveness of the search has not been declared, and records such as Thomas Flynn's probate file and a record of Patrick's birth remain unsearched; those would corroborate paternity. Maternity is **not proved**. This conclusion may change if new evidence appears.

narrative_markdown.before:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

narrative_markdown.after:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship-to-head column first appears in the 1880 census). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Did Person A (born 1856, Germany) leave an accessible South Dakota death certificate, and when did Person A die?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates that Person A died in 1935 and was buried at Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota. No death certificate is accessible in the indexed records searched, so the existence of a certificate is not established by the evidence gathered so far; this remains unresolved pending a request to the South Dakota State Archives or a browse of unindexed FamilySearch South Dakota death microfilm. The 1935 death year is a probable, bounded conclusion; the exact day is not known.

## Evidence
**Find a Grave Index** (derivative; information indeterminate, informant an unidentified contributor, stated): death 1935, Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota. Cited as: "Find a Grave Index," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVLD-NSQ7 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, memorial #88075502.

**South Dakota Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942** (original record; information indeterminate, informant unknown, burial stated, age inferred): burial at Gregory, Gregory County, age at death 79, date of death blank. Cited as: "South Dakota, Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942," database with images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:CYCQ-NRW2 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota. Age 79 with birth 1856 (tree fact F1, Birth, Germany, 1856, which carries no linked source entry in research.json) places death in 1935, or at the margin early 1936 if the unknown birth day fell late in 1856. This is indirect evidence; the earlier-stated 26 March bound assumes a birth date that is not in the record and is not relied on.

Tree fact F2 (Residence, Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota, 1935) places Person A there in 1935, consistent with both records; it carries no linked source entry in research.json.

## Correlation
Two sources with different origins (a contributor-built memorial index and a government grave register) agree on place (Gregory) and, via the age calculation, on the year. Neither names an exact death date and neither carries information from a known informant, so both are secondary in practice. The independence of the Find a Grave entry from the register is not demonstrated. No conflicts exist.

## Death certificate
Two indexed searches (two surname variants) returned only the derivative sources above. This is a negative result against the FamilySearch index only, not a finding that no certificate exists: South Dakota statewide death registration was in force in 1935, so a certificate may well exist unindexed. It would be held by the state and could refine or overturn the year.

## Tier
Probable: the year and place are consistently supported but by indeterminate-quality, indirect or derivative information, and reachable record types remain unsearched. Overturn risk is moderate.

## What could resolve it
A South Dakota State Archives / Department of Health request for a 1935 (or 1936) Gregory County death certificate; browsing unindexed FamilySearch South Dakota death microfilm; Gregory County newspapers and cemetery records (IOOF Cemetery).

Cited as: "Find a Grave Index," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVLD-NSQ7 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, memorial #88075502.

**South Dakota Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942** (original record; information indeterminate, informant unknown, burial stated, age inferred): burial at Gregory, Gregory County, age at death 79, date of death blank. Cited as: "South Dakota, Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942," database with images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:CYCQ-NRW2 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota. Age 79 with birth 1856 (tree fact F1, Birth, Germany, 1856, which carries no linked source entry in research.json) places death in 1935, or at the margin early 1936 if the unknown birth day fell late in 1856. This is indirect evidence; the earlier-stated 26 March bound assumes a birth date that is not in the record and is not relied on.

Tree fact F2 (Residence, Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota, 1935) places Person A there in 1935, consistent with both records; it carries no linked source entry in research.json.

## Correlation
Two sources with different origins (a contributor-built memorial index and a government grave register) agree on place (Gregory) and, via the age calculation, on the year. Neither names an exact death date and neither carries information from a known informant, so both are secondary in practice. The independence of the Find a Grave entry from the register is not demonstrated. No conflicts exist.

## Death certificate
Two indexed searches (two surname variants) returned only the derivative sources above. This is a negative result against the FamilySearch index only, not a finding that no certificate exists: South Dakota statewide death registration was in force in 1935, so a certificate may well exist unindexed. It would be held by the state and could refine or overturn the year.

## Tier
Probable: the year and place are consistently supported but by indeterminate-quality, indirect or derivative information, and reachable record types remain unsearched. Overturn risk is moderate.

## What could resolve it
A South Dakota State Archives / Department of Health request for a 1935 (or 1936) Gregory County death certificate; browsing unindexed FamilySearch South Dakota death microfilm; Gregory County newspapers and cemetery records (IOOF Cemetery).

The question of who Patrick Flynn's father was cannot be answered from the evidence gathered so far. Here is the full picture:

---

**What was found**

Two boys named Patrick Flynn of the right age appear in the 1850 census:
- One living in a household headed by **Thomas Flynn**
- One living in a household headed by **Michael Flynn**

Nothing in the evidence so far connects the adult Patrick to either household. By 1860 he appears as a boarder with no Flynn relatives nearby, and his **1908 death certificate left the father's name blank**. No baptism record was found in the parish registers.

---

**Conclusion — Not Proved** (`not_proved / gap`)

Neither Thomas Flynn nor Michael Flynn can currently be favored as Patrick's father. The proof summary (ps\_001) has been recorded as a proof argument at this tier, and question q\_001 remains open.

---

**What is still unsearched**

The following records were not yet consulted and could move the needle:
- **1870 and 1880 censuses** — Patrick may appear with or near a Flynn household
- **Records of Patrick's children** — their death certificates, obituaries, or marriages may name his parents
- **Patrick's own marriage or church record** — sometimes names the father
- **Probate/estate files for Thomas and Michael Flynn** — heirs named in a will could be decisive

**Recommended next step:** Route to `research-plan` to plan searches in those record sets.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908 Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Answer

Not proved. The evidence gathered so far does not favor Thomas Flynn over Michael Flynn, or either over a third man. Patrick's father is not established pending the record types named below.

## The two candidates

The 1850 U.S. census of Schuylkill County lists two Irish-born boys named Patrick Flynn of fitting age. One, age 5, is in the household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, family 91): 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The other, age 6, is in the household of Michael Flynn (dwelling 210, family 233, a different enumeration district): 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Both are original records. But the information in each is indeterminate: the informant is unknown, the 1850 census does not state relationships, and the child-of-head link is inferred from household position only. Age 5 (about 1845) and age 6 (about 1844) both fall within normal census age error for the subject. Each candidate is therefore equally weak: the link from the 1850 boy to our Patrick is an assumption, not evidence, and the two cannot be told apart.

## The bridging records do not bridge

The 1860 census shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, a boarder and coal laborer in the Owen Donnelly household (dwelling 305), with no Flynn adult present: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. This is original, with the enumerator as witness to residence, but it names no relative, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor. It is consistent with either candidate, and with a Patrick from neither household.

The 1908 death certificate is unambiguously the subject: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026. The death date and place are primary information from the attending physician. The father's name is blank; the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported it as unknown. This is negative evidence: the one record at the end of life that should name the father does not, and the informant was too distant to know. It adds nothing toward either candidate.

The search of Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland, Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) located no baptism naming a father. That is a not-found result in indexes of uncertain coverage, not proof that no such record exists.

## Why no tier above not proved

Two candidates, one hypothesis each (Thomas, Michael), no evidence that separates them, and no direct evidence of parentage anywhere. No conflict is registered, because the sources do not contradict each other; they simply fail to connect to one another. A pick between the two would rest on coin-flip odds, so neither is concluded and nothing is written to the tree as a parent-child link.

## What could resolve it

# Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908 Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Answer

Not proved. The evidence gathered so far does not favor Thomas Flynn over Michael Flynn, or either over a third man. Patrick's father is not established pending the record types named below.

## The two candidates

The 1850 U.S. census of Schuylkill County lists two Irish-born boys named Patrick Flynn of fitting age. One, age 5, is in the household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, family 91): 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The other, age 6, is in the household of Michael Flynn (dwelling 210, family 233, a different enumeration district): 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Both are original records. But the information in each is indeterminate: the informant is unknown, the 1850 census does not state relationships, and the child-of-head link is inferred from household position only. Age 5 (about 1845) and age 6 (about 1844) both fall within normal census age error for the subject. Each candidate is therefore equally weak: the link from the 1850 boy to our Patrick is an assumption, not evidence, and the two cannot be told apart.

## The bridging records do not bridge

The 1860 census shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, a boarder and coal laborer in the Owen Donnelly household (dwelling 305), with no Flynn adult present: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. This is original, with the enumerator as witness to residence, but it names no relative, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor. It is consistent with either candidate, and with a Patrick from neither household.

The 1908 death certificate is unambiguously the subject: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026. The death date and place are primary information from the attending physician. The father's name is blank; the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported it as unknown. This is negative evidence: the one record at the end of life that should name the father does not, and the informant was too distant to know. It adds nothing toward either candidate.

The search of Catholic parish registers (FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland, Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) located no baptism naming a father. That is a not-found result in indexes of uncertain coverage, not proof that no such record exists.

## Why no tier above not proved

Two candidates, one hypothesis each (Thomas, Michael), no evidence that separates them, and no direct evidence of parentage anywhere. No conflict is registered, because the sources do not contradict each other; they simply fail to connect to one another. A pick between the two would rest on coin-flip odds, so neither is concluded and nothing is written to the tree as a parent-child link.

## What could resolve it

This is unresolved on the current record set, not unresolvable. Records not yet searched that could narrow the answer: the 1870 and 1880 censuses for Patrick (a Flynn elder or relatives in or beside his household); death certificates, obituaries and marriage records of Patrick's children, which may name their grandfather; Patrick's own marriage or church record; and Schuylkill County estate or probate files for Thomas and Michael Flynn that might name a son Patrick. Tracing what became of Thomas and Michael Flynn after 1850 could also eliminate one of them. Any of these could favor a candidate, and the first three could name the father outright. Proofs are never final; a new record could change this finding.
